questions.topic: Frontend vs backend vs database; web development workflow
questions.text: What does MERN stand for, and what role does each part play?
questions.ideal_answer: MERN stands for MongoDB, Express.js, React and Node.js. MongoDB is a NoSQL document database that stores data as JSON-like documents. Express.js is a web framework running on Node.js that handles routing, middleware and REST APIs on the server. React is a JavaScript library for building the user interface in the browser. Node.js is the JavaScript runtime that runs the backend server, so the whole stack uses JavaScript.

questions.topic: React: components, JSX, props, state, hooks
questions.ideal_answer: JSX stands for JavaScript XML and is a syntax extension that lets us write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript code. It is used in React to describe what the user interface should look like. Browsers cannot read JSX directly, so a tool like Babel compiles it into React.createElement calls or the newer JSX runtime functions. JavaScript expressions can be embedded in JSX using curly braces, and attributes use camelCase such as className.

questions.text: What is the difference between props and state in React?
questions.ideal_answer: Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child component, and they are read-only inside the child. State is data managed inside a component that can change over time, usually through the useState hook in function components. When state changes, React re-renders the component. Data flows down from parent to child through props, and a child can ask the parent to change data by calling a function passed as a prop.

questions.topic: HTML5, CSS3, Flexbox, Grid and responsive design
questions.text: What is the difference between CSS Flexbox and CSS Grid?
questions.ideal_answer: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system that arranges items along a single row or a single column, with properties like justify-content and align-items. CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system that controls rows and columns at the same time using grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. Flexbox is ideal for components like navigation bars and aligning items in a line. Grid is better for whole page layouts. Both are often used together and with media queries for responsive design.

questions.topic: Express.js routing, middleware and REST APIs
questions.text: What is middleware in Express.js, and how does a request pass through it?
questions.ideal_answer: Middleware is a function with access to the request object, the response object and the next function. Middleware runs in the order it is registered with app.use or on routes. Each middleware can read or modify the request and response, end the request by sending a response, or call next() to pass control to the next middleware. Common uses include parsing JSON with express.json, logging, authentication checks and error handling. Error-handling middleware takes four arguments, with err as the first.

questions.text: How would you define a schema and perform basic CRUD operations on users with Mongoose?
questions.ideal_answer: First, define a schema with new mongoose.Schema, listing fields like name, email and password with their types and validations such as required and unique. Then create a model with mongoose.model('User', userSchema), which maps to a users collection. For create we use User.create or new User().save(), for read we use find or findById, for update findByIdAndUpdate, and for delete findByIdAndDelete. These methods return promises, so they are used with async and await and wrapped in try-catch for errors.

questions.text: Node.js is single-threaded. Why can it still handle thousands of concurrent requests, and when does it perform badly?
questions.ideal_answer: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single main thread with an event loop and uses non-blocking, asynchronous I/O. When a request needs a database query or file read, Node hands the work to the operating system or the libuv thread pool and continues serving other requests; when the result is ready, a callback is queued and processed by the event loop. This makes it very efficient for I/O-bound workloads like APIs. It performs badly for CPU-intensive tasks such as image processing or heavy calculations, because they block the event loop and delay all other requests. Such work should go to worker threads or separate services.

questions.topic: JavaScript ES6+: arrow functions, promises, async/await
questions.text: What is printed by: console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D'); and why?
questions.ideal_answer: The output is A, D, C, B. First the synchronous code runs, printing A and D. The promise callback is placed in the microtask queue and the setTimeout callback is placed in the macrotask or task queue. After the synchronous code finishes, the event loop runs all microtasks before the next macrotask, so C is printed before B. A zero millisecond timeout does not run immediately; it only waits for the call stack and microtasks to clear.

questions.text: How would you implement secure login in a MERN app with JWT, and what mistakes should you avoid?
questions.ideal_answer: On sign-up, the password is hashed with a slow salted algorithm like bcrypt before saving, never stored in plain text. On login, the server compares the password with the hash using bcrypt.compare, and if it matches it signs a JWT containing the user id with a secret key and a short expiry. The client sends the token in the Authorization header as a Bearer token, or it is kept in an httpOnly secure cookie, and middleware verifies it on protected routes. Mistakes to avoid are storing sensitive data in the payload, since it is only encoded not encrypted, hard-coding the secret, using no expiry, and storing tokens in localStorage where XSS can steal them. Refresh tokens can be used for longer sessions.

questions.topic: Connecting React to Node with Axios/Fetch; CORS
questions.text: Your React app on localhost:3000 calls your Express API on localhost:5000 and the browser shows a CORS error. Why does this happen and how do you fix it?
questions.ideal_answer: The two URLs have different ports, so they are different origins, and the browser's same-origin policy blocks the frontend from reading the response unless the server allows it. CORS is a mechanism where the server sends headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin to say which origins may access it. The fix is on the server: use the cors middleware in Express with origin set to the frontend URL, and credentials true if cookies are sent. For requests with custom headers or methods, the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request, which must also be allowed. In development, a proxy setting in the React dev server is another option; disabling CORS in the browser is not a real fix.

questions.topic: State management: Context API and Redux
questions.text: Your team's React app passes user and cart data through many layers of components and is becoming hard to maintain. Would you use Context API or Redux, and why?
questions.ideal_answer: Passing props through many intermediate components is called prop drilling, and both Context API and Redux solve it by providing a shared global state. Context API is built into React and is good for simple, rarely changing data like the logged-in user, theme or language. However, every consumer re-renders when the context value changes, so it is less efficient for frequently changing state. Redux, especially Redux Toolkit, offers a single store, predictable updates through actions and reducers, middleware for async logic and excellent DevTools, which suits a large and frequently updated cart state. A common choice is Context for auth and theme and Redux Toolkit for complex app state.

questions.topic: Deployment and Security: OWASP Top 10, rate limiting, environment variables
questions.text: You are about to deploy a MERN app to production. What security and deployment practices would you follow?
questions.ideal_answer: Secrets such as the database URL and JWT secret must be kept in environment variables configured on the host, like Render or Vercel, and never committed to Git. I would enforce HTTPS, add security headers with helmet, and restrict CORS to the real frontend domain. Following the OWASP Top 10, all input should be validated and sanitised to prevent NoSQL injection and XSS, and passwords hashed with bcrypt. Rate limiting with express-rate-limit protects login routes from brute force. The database should use least-privilege credentials and IP restrictions, dependencies should be checked with npm audit, and errors should be logged without leaking stack traces to users.
